title: Algorithm Viewer v2.0.0

**Author**: Yulric Sequeira \
**Version:** 2.0.0 \
**Created:** 12/11/2025 \

## Abstract

The aim of the algorithm viewer is to enable users to gain a deeper
understanding of their models. It accomplishes this by displaying the
relationship between the predictors and outcome of a model using intuitive and
interactive visualizations in a web-based application. The ever-increasing
complexity of models—both in terms of the algorithms used to fit them and the
number and intricacy of predictors—makes applications such as these an essential
part of the model-building toolkit

## Motivation

The rise of big data has enabled the increase in model complexity which can
improve model performance. The use of machine learning algorithms to fit a
model, the inclusion of a large number of predictors, the use of transformations
like splining and scaling, and the inclusion of interaction terms, all of these
methods can increase the complexity of a model. Due to their complexity, these
models are treated as a black box as it is no longer humanly possible to hand
calculate the outcome or to understand the predictor-outcome relationships using
the model coefficients. As more of these models are integrated into practice the
lack of understanding can lead to model issues being overlooked especially in
under-represented sections of the population. As such, there is a growing need
for tools that are able to better explain how these models work in essence
opening up the black box. The algorithm viewer aims to be one such tool.

## Specifications

The goal of this version of the viewer is to improve the understanding of models
with interactions terms. The models for the Hypertension Population Risk Tool or
HTNPoRT will be used for this version. More details about HTNPoRT can be seen in
its [repo](https://github.com/Big-Life-Lab/htnport). Relevant details are that
HTNPoRT consists of two models, one for males and one for females both of which
are logistic regression. The outcome of the model is the probability that an
individual has hypertension. The model has two way age interaction terms. Odds
ratio curves over the age range of the models for each predictor will be used to
meet the goal stated above. This version of the viewer will effectively be
recreating the bottom left visualization of the
[previous viewer](https://algorithm-viewer.projectbiglife.ca/#/cvdport-r) but
for logistic regression models.

### Predictor Transformations

**Objective:** Optionally apply transformations to input vectors before passing
them to the model when calculating odds ratio curves.

- **Supported Transformations:**
  - Centering: Center a predictor by subtracting a centering value.
  - Dummy: Create binary dummy variables from categorical predictors.
  - Restricted Cubic Splines: Transform a predictor with a restricted cubic
    spline.
  - Interactions: Multiply two or more predictors to create a derived
    interaction term.
  - Logistic: Apply a logistic equation using an intercept and coefficients.

- **Transformation Specification:**
  - Should comply with the transformations specified in the
    [Model Parameters](https://github.com/Big-Life-Lab/model-parameters)
    repository.
  - Full specification for input transformations is found in the [Predictor
    Transformations Specification](predictor-transformations-spec.qmd)
    document.

### Odds Ratio Curves

**Objective:** Generate interactive visualizations showing how odds
ratios change across age for predictors for both models.

- **Basic Visualization:**
  - X-axis: Age (continuous scale)
  - Y-axis: Odds ratio (OR) for the selected predictor
  - OR value at each age represents: the odds of the outcome in the exposed
    versus the unexposed group at that specific age. For categorical predictors,
    the unexposed group is the reference category. For continuous predictors,
    use a one-unit increase in the predictor value as the reference.

- **Predictor:**
  - From the perspective of the viewer and the user, the predictors are the
    variables in the model as they appear in the study dataset after the
    inclusion/exclusion criteria have been applied but before any model specific
    transformations have been applied.
  - The implication of this is that model variables may not necessarily be a
    predictor from the perspective of the viewer
  - For example, if a model has 5 variables, three of which are spline terms for
    centered age and one of which is a dummy variable for centered males, then
    for the viewer the predictors are age before centering and splining and the
    categories for sex before centering

- **Categorical Predictors:**
  - Each category visualized as a separate OR curve
  - All curves compared against the reference category (OR = 1)
  - Reference category labeled clearly
  - Only show non-reference categories

- **Continuous Predictor:**
  - In each curve, the odds ratio value at each age should be calculated for a
    unit-increase in the value of the predictor

- **Age Range Configuration:**
  - Use age range from metadata (minimum and maximum)
  - Generate smooth curves by calculating OR at appropriate intervals
    (e.g., every year)

- **Curve Generation:**
   - Use model coefficients and age values to compute OR at each point
   - Visualize as a continuous line (not discrete points) for
     each predictors

- **Sex support:**
  - The application should show the visualization for both models for all
    predictors

- **Visualization Data:**
  - Data needed for the visualization should ideally be standardized in a format
    that is human-readable/editable and machine actionable. The data should be
    imported into the application and used to render the visualizations. Avoid
    hardcoding as much as possible.
  - The [model-parameters](https://github.com/Big-Life-Lab/model-parameters)
    project contains structures for different piece of the model that can be
    used. New pieces of data needed by the application should be added to
    model-parameters project.
  - A data validation workflow should be put in place to ensure correctness. Any
    errors should contain enough metadata to inform users where the errors are
    as well as instructions on how to fix them

### Deployment

**Objective:** Ensure the application can be statically hosted and runs
reliably in browsers

- **Statically Hosted**
  - Ideally the application would not require a server other than to serve
    the application itself
  - Tools like [R shinylive](https://posit-dev.github.io/r-shinylive/) can help
    with this
- **Github Pages**
  - This version of the viewer should be built with the assumption that it will
    be hosted on Github pages
- **Browsers**
  - The viewer should run reliably on Chrome with support for other browser to
    come later

### Integrated Tutorial and Documentation

**Objective:** Help users understand what the application does and how to
use it.

- **Tutorial Content (Built into Application):**
  - **What is the Algorithm Viewer?** - Brief explanation of
    the application purpose and use cases
  - **Why was it developed?** - Explain the goal of understanding how
    predictors affect outcomes in prediction models, with specific focus
    on interaction effects
  - **How to use it** - Step-by-step guide including:
    - How to interpret the resulting OR curve
    - What interaction terms mean in the context of the visualization

- **Audience Assumption:**
  - Assume users have statistical background knowledge
  - Define technical terms (odds ratio, interaction term) but don't
    over-explain basic statistical concepts

- **Accessibility from UI:**
  - Tutorial must be easily accessible from the main application
    interface (e.g., help button, info panel)
  - Option to view tutorial without affecting current visualization

## Conclusion

The aim of the viewer is to open up the black box of complex models to gain a
deeper understanding of their inner workings. To start with, this version of the
viewer will focus on interactions terms using HTNPoRT as the use-case. The
viewer is a web-based application that will use odds ratio curves to meet this
goal. The application should use existing data standards to power the
visualizations and should be deployable to Github pages. The viewer should be
seen as one of the tools in a model builders toolkit to better understand their
models.
